title: the water before the words
hook: washing before prayer: why these parts, in this order

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-Fatiha, a conversation, answered line by line. Today, what comes before a single word of it.

Near the door of many mosques there's a row of taps along a wall, a low ledge to sit on, a drain along the floor. Before the prayer, people stop here first. Sleeves up, shoes off. Water over the hands, into the mouth, over the face, up the arms, over the feet. If you grew up with it, you could do it with your eyes closed. So: why these parts, and why this order?
screen: `A ROW OF TAPS BY THE DOOR.` → `HANDS, FACE, ARMS, FEET.` → `WHY THESE? WHY THIS ORDER?`

segments.voice: It's called wudu, from a root with the sense of brightness, the way a washed face shines. The core is one verse of the Qur'an: “When ye rise up for prayer, wash your faces, and your hands up to the elbows,” then wipe the head, and then the feet. Face, arms, head, feet: that's the order, and it comes from the verse itself. The rest, the hands first, the mouth and nose, the ears, families learned from the way the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ showed his companions. Here's the surprising part. It isn't really about dirt. People make wudu when they're already clean. A saying of the Prophet pictures it this way: as the water runs off your face, the wrongs your eyes looked at run off with it; off the hands, what the hands did; off the feet, where the feet went. So it's a reset, done with the body: the step between the street and the prayer. It lasts until something breaks it, like sleep, so it isn't always a fresh wash for every prayer. And when there's no water, or water would harm you, the same verse allows clean earth instead. That's called tayammum. The reset is never out of reach.
screen: `WUDU — FROM A ROOT OF BRIGHTNESS.` · `FACE, ARMS, HEAD, FEET.` · `THE WRONGS RUN OFF WITH THE WATER.` · `NO WATER? CLEAN EARTH.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. If there's water near you, wash your hands slowly and feel it run off your fingers. If not, rest your hands open and picture cool water over them, then over your face. With each breath out, let one thing from today run off with it.
Wudu. The washing before prayer: face, arms, head and feet. A reset with water. Third word.
Your line: rinse the day off. The day doesn't have to come with you into the prayer. Day three.

howItsDone: Muslims make wudu before prayer unless they are still in a state of wudu from an earlier washing; mosques have washing areas with taps, and at home it's done at an ordinary sink.

original.note: Arabic: the washing before prayer, from a root of brightness and cleanness.

trapdoor: what you thought: washing up before praying, like manners.
what it means: wudu — a set washing of face, arms, head and feet that turns the body toward prayer.
what a scholar hears: a root of brightness; one verse (5:6) gives the four core parts in order, the Prophet's practice fills in the rest, and the same verse provides tayammum.

story.title: footsteps ahead in paradise
story.text: After the dawn prayer one day, the Prophet ﷺ turns to Bilal, a freed slave, with a strange question. I heard your footsteps ahead of me in paradise, he says. What have you been doing? Bilal thinks it over. Nothing much, he says: only that whenever I make wudu, by day or by night, I pray with it.

wrong.truth: people make it when they're already clean. it's a reset: the step between the street and the prayer.

think.reveal: the water isn't about dirt. it's the step between the street and the prayer, and it works best slowly.

notes: Moved: old day 13 → day 3 (the audience research's #2 moment: why these parts, in this order). Tightened; the practice is now three breaths.

Week one leaves out the Sunni/Shia difference on the feet (washed or wiped) and the other differences in how the arms are washed; the voice says only 'then the feet', which fits both readings of 5:6. The earlier script named the difference; it can come back in a later camp. Confirm.

'Families learned the rest (hands first, mouth and nose, ears) from the way the Prophet showed his companions': the order is the common one; schools differ on which of these are required and which recommended. Confirm the phrasing is fair to both Sunni and Shia practice.

'It lasts until something breaks it, like sleep': what breaks wudu differs in detail between the schools (e.g. kinds of sleep); the script names only sleep, which all treat as breaking it in its deep form. Confirm.
